Show Me the Receipts  ·  Field Note  ·  October 2026

Warmth Opens the Door.
It Doesn’t Keep It Open.

Why “fundraising is about relationships” stops one step too early

Glen E. Quiring, CFRE  ·  ShowMeReceipts.org

What the research found first

The coaching profession has been working this question longer than fundraising has. Graßmann, Schölmerich, and Schermuly pooled 27 studies covering more than 3,500 coaching engagements and found that relationship quality predicted outcomes — meaningfully. Researchers express that as r = .41. In behavioral research, where most single factors move the needle modestly, that number holds up.

But a second study cut deeper. Gessnitzer and Kauffeld videotaped 31 real coaching relationships and coded what was actually happening inside them. Bonding behavior on its own did not predict success. What predicted it was the client taking ownership of goals and direction. When the coach drove that agreement, results went the other way.

The relationship matters. Warmth is not the part doing the work.

“Fundraising is about relationships” is a true observation pointing at the wrong mechanism.

The same structure in fundraising

A watershed isn’t a thing you can point to on a map. It’s the entire upstream system — snowpack, hillside, forest floor, tributary — that determines what a river carries. The river is just the channel. That image does something the fundraising literature hasn’t quite managed.

Warmth creates the opening. The record is what keeps it open.

Consider a donor who feels a strong connection with their fundraiser. Later they discover their gift was misused, their intent ignored, the promised impact never materialized. The relationship got them in the room. The institutional record determined whether they stayed.

This is the move the folklore does not make. When we say fundraising is about relationships, we locate trust in the person. That is partly true and dangerously incomplete. Trust is an institutional record of kept promises. The fundraiser carries that record into every conversation, for better or worse. The fundraiser is the river. What flows through the conversation depends on everything upstream.

The Distinction in Plain Terms
Relationship quality Gets you in the room. Predicts whether the donor engages. It is the river.
Institutional record Keeps you in the room. Predicts whether the donor stays. It is the watershed.

What this means in practice

The question “how is my relationship with this donor?” is necessary but not sufficient. The more complete question: what is the institutional record this donor has accumulated, and does it match what we promised them?

When a major donor lapses, the failure may not be relational. It may be the relationship between the organization and its own stated commitments.

The most valuable thing you can carry into a donor conversation is a clear account of what was promised and what was delivered. That is the receipt. That is what trust is made of.

About this field note

Glen E. Quiring, CFRE, is the Director of Philanthropy at the Allan Hancock College Foundation and the developer of Show Me the Receipts, a fundraising trust framework. Field Notes are practitioner observations in the SMTR series — short-form pieces written from the floor, not the podium.

Research note: The 27-study figure is from Graßmann, C., Schölmerich, F., & Schermuly, C. C. (2020). The relationship between working alliance and client outcomes in coaching: A meta-analysis. Human Relations, 73(1), 35–58. https://doi.org/10.1177/0018726718819725. Meta-analysis of 27 samples, N = 3,563 coaching processes. Overall working alliance–outcome correlation: r = .41 (95% CI .34 to .48); squared, about 17% of the variance in outcomes. The behavior finding is from Gessnitzer, S., & Kauffeld, S. (2015). The working alliance in coaching: Why behavior is the key to success. The Journal of Applied Behavioral Science, 51(2), 177–197. https://doi.org/10.1177/0021886315576407. Thirty-one coaching dyads, sessions videotaped and coded: client-initiated agreement on goals and tasks predicted success; bonding behavior did not; coach-initiated agreement had the opposite effect. Both studies concern coaching. Applying them to donors is an analogy, not a finding, and neither shows that relationship quality predicts institutional trust.
